title: Weak prefix-based type deny list in ParserConfig (default only blocks java.lang.Thread) does not prevent arbitrary class-name @type usage
description:
ParserConfig.getDeserializer(Class, Type) performs a blacklist check on the resolved class name: it derives className = clazz.getName().replace('$','.') and iterates denyList, throwing JSONException("parser deny : ...") when className.startsWith(deny) (lines 360-367). The default denyList is a single entry {"java.lang.Thread"} (line 147), and it is only extended by addDeny (lines 696-705), addItemsToDeny(DENYS) at construction (lines 263-264), readSystemDenyPropety() (lines 288-291) and configFromPropety (lines 273-277), i.e. by operator-supplied system property fastjson.parser.deny or explicit API calls.

Security relevance: the guard is (a) an opt-in, extremely narrow blacklist rather than an allowlist, and (b) applied as a substring/prefix match, so it does not restrict classes outside java.lang.Thread by default. Any type name not matching the currently-configured deny entries proceeds to normal deserializer resolution (including java.awt.* at lines 369-384, java.time.*/java.util.Optional* at lines 386-417, and generic JavaBean deserialization at lines 447-462). Where a caller-supplied type name reaches getDeserializer, the deny list is not a positive type-safety boundary. Note the check is also evaluated on the already-resolved Class, so it cannot prevent whatever happens while the Class is being obtained; only its reachability from the @type parsing path is unverified here.

title: ParserConfig unconditionally initializes runtime ASM bytecode generation for deserialization
description:
The ParserConfig constructor sets up an ASMDeserializerFactory backed by an ASMClassLoader (lines 161-178): if no factory is supplied and the platform is not Android, it instantiates ASMDeserializerFactory(new ASMClassLoader()) or with the given parent ClassLoader, with asmEnable defaulting to true (line 134). asmEnable is only turned off on failure (lines 180-182) or when specific reflection-based conditions are met (lines 579-583, non-static member classes). createJavaBeanDeserializer then prefers asmFactory.createJavaBeanDeserializer (line 591) and falls back to JavaBeanDeserializer on NoSuchMethodException (lines 595-596).

Security relevance: deserialization dynamically generates and loads bytecode based on the target class's bean metadata instead of only instantiating beans reflectively. This is an ASM/classloader trust surface that is enabled by default rather than being opt-in. The exception handling in the constructor swallows ExceptionInInitializerError/AccessControlException/NoClassDefFoundError silently (lines 169-175), which can mask environment-based disablement of the ASM path.

title: Polymorphic @type deserialization in DefaultJSONParser resolves and instantiates attacker-supplied classes with only a weak prefix denylist guard
description:
In DefaultJSONParser.parseObject(Map, Object), when a parsed field name equals JSON.DEFAULT_TYPE_KEY ("@type") and Feature.DisableSpecialKeyDetect is disabled, the code reads a string value via lexer.scanSymbol and resolves it to a Class with TypeUtils.loadClass(typeName, config.getDefaultClassLoader()) (lines 320-322). The resolved Class is then: (i) passed to config.getDeserializer(clazz) and deserializer.deserialze(this, clazz, fieldName) (lines 367-368), and (ii) in the RBRACE branch used for instantiation via ((JavaBeanDeserializer) deserializer).createInstance(this, clazz) or, if that yields null, clazz.newInstance() (lines 333-346). There is no allowlist at the call site.

The only filtering visible in the read source is in ParserConfig.getDeserializer(Class<?> clazz, Type type): it derives className = clazz.getName() with '$' replaced by '.', removes the JSONType.mappingTo indirection/resolution, and then loops over denyList throwing JSONException only when className.startsWith(deny) (lines 360-367). The default denyList is new String[] { "java.lang.Thread" } (line 147), augmented in the constructor with addDeny("java.lang.Thread") and addItemsToDeny(DENYS), where DENYS is loaded from the system property "fastjson.parser.deny" (lines 122-124, 263-265, 288-291). This is a denylist with a raw prefix match, so every class not explicitly denied is accepted. Additionally, the deny check is placed after the derializers cache lookups (lines 306-340) and is not invoked from the @type branch before loadClass, so the class is resolved first and only then possibly filtered. Because addDeny/addItemsToDeny are public (lines 273-286) and the deny list is a mutable array replaced on each addition, the guard is also programmatically adjustable. The net effect visible in these spans is that a JSON document containing "@type" can direct the parser to a deserializer or to reflection-based instantiation for essentially any class on the classpath that is not in a one-entry (plus system-property) deny list.

title: Deny check applies a raw prefix match after cache lookups and is decoupled from class resolution in getDeserializer
description:
ParserConfig.getDeserializer(Class<?> clazz, Type type) performs several derializers map lookups first (identity by Type, then by clazz, plus the JSONType.mappingTo redirect at lines 343-350, plus a clazz lookup for wildcard/type-variable/parameterized types at lines 352-358). Only after these can the denyList loop be reached (lines 360-367). Two consequences are visible in the read source: (a) any type whose deserializer was already registered in the derializers map (including all the built-ins registered in the constructor, lines 184-261, and anything inserted later through getDerializers()/put) returns early at lines 306-340 and never reaches the deny check; (b) the deny check compares className.startsWith(deny) on the dotted class name, which is a prefix rather than an exact/allowlist comparison, so a deny entry matches a whole family of names and, conversely, a class not sharing the denied prefix bypasses the check entirely.

Separately, in DefaultJSONParser the class value from "@type" is resolved by TypeUtils.loadClass before any getDeserializer call (line 322) and is only later passed to getDeserializer (lines 334 and 367), so class resolution itself is not guarded by the denyList in the read spans. Whether TypeUtils.loadClass applies its own restrictions cannot be confirmed from the allowed spans.

title: Deny list is extensible and mutable at runtime, allowing the classification guard to be modified programmatically
description: ParserConfig exposes addDeny(String) and addItemsToDeny(String[]) as public/modifiable operations that append to a private String[] denyList by allocating a new array and copying (lines 273-286 and the addDeny body reported by search in the same class). label: flash_max
title: Type-name deny list in ParserConfig is minimal and its prefix check is applied to the '$'-normalized name, weakening class-name blocklisting
description:
In ParserConfig the blocklist-based guard for type-name-driven deserialization is weak in two ways that are visible in the read source.

(a) Minimal default policy: the class field denyList is initialized to only {"java.lang.Thread"} (line 147). The constructor calls addDeny("java.lang.Thread") (line 263) and addItemsToDeny(DENYS) (line 264), where DENYS is populated from the JVM system property "fastjson.parser.deny" via readSystemDenyPropety() -> IOUtils.getStringProperty(DENY_PROPERTY) (lines 122-124, 288-291). There is no built-in list of dangerous classes (no JDK/JNDI/rowset/gadget entries) in this source. Consequently the effective protection depends entirely on an external system property and, by default, blocks a single class name.

(b) Prefix matching against a normalized name: the deny enforcement in getDeserializer(Class, Type) computes `String className = clazz.getName(); className = className.replace('$', '.');` (lines 360-361) and then, for each deny entry, throws only if `className.startsWith(deny)` (lines 362-367). Because the compared name has '$' replaced by '.', any deny entry that itself contains '$' (e.g. a property-supplied inner-class name) can never match the normalized className, so such entries silently fail to block. Conversely the check remains a raw startsWith prefix test, so it is a name-shape heuristic rather than an authoritative type restriction.

The net effect within the read spans is that the only type-name restriction mechanism present is a short, configuration-fallible prefix blocklist evaluated on a normalized class name, while the class->deserializer selection that follows (lines 442-464, including createJavaBeanDeserializer at 469+) will build a deserializer for any class that is not caught by this list. Whether an attacker-controlled type string can actually reach this guard, and whether a deserializer for a dangerous class is then instantiated, depends on callers outside the read spans (DefaultJSONParser/TypeUtils/JavaBeanDeserializer were not read as source), so this is reported as a candidate weakness in the guard's design, not as a demonstrated vulnerability.

title: Weak/prefix-only denyList for autoType class filtering

title: SAXDocumentFactory does not disable DOCTYPE processing (no disallow-doctype-decl); relies solely on external-entity features
description: SAXDocumentFactory initializes a SAXParserFactory and disables external-general-entities and external-parameter-entities (lines 402-411), and re-applies those features plus namespaces/validation on the created XMLReader (lines 441-448). title: DefaultScriptSecurity host check can be bypassed when both hosts are null (identity comparison + null-host short-circuit)
description: DefaultScriptSecurity's constructor compares the document host and the script host using reference identity (docHost != scriptHost) OR'ed with a null-aware equals test. The security decision is made only inside the `if ((docHost != scriptHost) && ((docHost == null) || (!docHost.equals(scriptHost))))` block (lines 87-88). When the two host strings are the same interned/identical reference, or when docHost is non-null and docHost.equals(scriptHost) is true, the block is not entered and `se` stays null, so checkLoadScript() returns silently. More importantly for null hosts: if docHost is null, the second clause `(docHost == null)` evaluates true, but that only broadens when the block is entered; the guard is bypassed entirely only when the identity test is false. Because `ParsedURL.getHost()` can return null for several URL shapes (e.g. file:, data:, and relative/opaque references), and because scripts embedded with the data protocol are explicitly exempted (lines 89-93), a document that is itself loaded from a null-host URL can accept a script reference to a different location without triggering the cross-host SecurityException. The intent of the class (only allow scripts from the same server as the document) is therefore not enforced for null-host inputs. This is reported as a candidate; traceability to a concrete attacker-controlled entry point is not established in the read source.

title: XML parser hardening in XmlConverter is best-effort and silently degrades (no disallow-doctype-decl / external-parameter-entities)
description: XmlConverter.createDocumentBuilderFactory() is the central factory used by the DOM/SAX conversion methods (toDOMDocument, toDOMSource, etc.) that parse message bodies and headers. The setupFeatures() helper allows arbitrary feature URIs to be injected via system properties named org.apache.camel.xmlconverter.documentBuilderFactory.feature, which could also re-enable entity processing, but that requires control of JVM system properties rather than message input. This is reported as a hardening/config weakness; I could not demonstrate an end-to-end untrusted input path or confirm the effective provider behavior statically.

description:
XmlConverter.createDocumentBuilderFactory() is the factory behind the DOM converters such as toDOMDocument(File, Exchange) (lines 943-946: getDocumentBuilderFactory(exchange).newDocumentBuilder() then documentBuilder.parse(file)) and the byte[]-to-Document converter (toDOMDocument(byte[], Exchange) calls getDocumentBuilderFactory(exchange).newDocumentBuilder() and parse). The hardening applied in the read span is:
- namespaceAware / ignoringElementContentWhitespace / ignoringComments (1101-1103)
- setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false) inside a try/catch that only logs a warning (1104-1110)
- best-effort install of org.apache.xerces.util.SecurityManager for Apache Xerces, with the whole block wrapped in a catch(Exception) that only logs (1111-1122)
- setupFeatures(factory) applying any system property starting with org.apache.camel.xmlconverter.documentBuilderFactory.feature, where a failing setFeature is caught and only warned (1057-1085)

Root cause / weakness: none of these protections is enforced. If the underlying parser does not support a given feature/attribute, the exception is swallowed and parsing proceeds with the protection absent, while the log message is informational only. In this span only external-general-entities is explicitly disabled; there is no disallow-doctype-decl or external-parameter-entities handling, and no secure-processing feature is set here. label: flash_high
title: Expander path check uses a string prefix test on canonical paths, allowing escape into a sibling directory whose name starts with the target directory name
description: Expander.expand(ArchiveEntrySupplier, EntryWriter, File) is the common extraction routine used by all expand(...) overloads (ZIP via ZipFile, 7z via SevenZFile, streaming via ArchiveInputStream). It computes the target directory's canonical path once (line 241) and, for every entry, builds `new File(targetDirectory, nextEntry.getName())` (line 244). The containment check at line 245 is `!f.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(targetDirPath)`. This is a plain String prefix comparison on a canonical path, not a comparison of path components (no separator appended to the prefix, no Path.startsWith/normalize check). As a result, for a target directory whose canonical path is `/base/out/x`, an entry name such as `../xy/evil` resolves to canonical path `/base/out/xy/evil`, which does satisfy startsWith(`/base/out/x`), so no IOException is thrown and the file is written outside the target directory via Files.newOutputStream(f.toPath()) at line 258 (data written at line 259). The entry name is attacker-controlled archive metadata (set from the local/central header name field for ZIP, from the tar name field for tar, etc.), so an archive with such a name causes file creation outside the intended directory. The exact same weakness is described in the repository's own release notes for the unreleased 1.18 release (changes.xml lines 47-52: 'The example Expander class has been vulnerable to a path traversal in the edge case that happens when the target directory has a sibling directory and the name of the target directory is a prefix of the sibling directory's name.'), which corroborates the mechanism from repository data. title: Unbounded in-memory caching of STORED entries with data descriptor in ZipArchiveInputStream.readStoredEntry
description: In ZipArchiveInputStream.readStoredEntry() (lines 877-906) the stream reads until it detects a local-file-header / central-directory-header / data-descriptor signature and writes every byte it consumes into a ByteArrayOutputStream (bos). title: Mis-indexed central-directory signature test in ZipArchiveInputStream.bufferContainsSignature defeats CDH detection for stored entries with data descriptors
description:
In bufferContainsSignature() the outer guard at line 926 matches the PK (0x50 0x4B) prefix, and the inner condition at lines 927-928 is meant to accept either a local file header signature (PK\x03\x04) or a central directory header signature (PK\x01\x02). Data descriptor signatures (PK\x07\x08, tested at 933-937) and LFH signatures are still detected, so only a following central-directory header is missed. title: DumpArchiveInputStream may allocate heap and iterate based on unbounded attacker-controlled header count
description:
DumpArchiveInputStream parses UNIX dump archives from an untrusted InputStream. In the constructor and in entry-iteration paths it reads attacker-controlled headers and uses the header's count/size fields to drive heap allocation and read/skip loops:

- readCLRI()/readBITS() skip `TP_SIZE * active.getHeaderCount()` bytes (lines 188, 212).
- getNextEntry() skips `TP_SIZE * (active.getHeaderCount() - active.getHeaderHoles())` (lines 267-269) and individually skips `TP_SIZE` per non-sparse record while `readIdx < active.getHeaderCount()` (lines 247-251).
- readDirectoryEntry() computes `datalen = TP_SIZE * entry.getHeaderCount()` and, if the current blockBuffer is smaller, replaces it with `new byte[datalen]`, then reads exactly that many bytes (lines 341-349).

If `getHeaderCount()` is taken directly from the record without an upper-bound/sanity check relative to the actual stream length, a small crafted archive declaring a very large count could cause a large single heap allocation and/or a long read/skip loop, i.e. resource-consumption behavior driven by untrusted input. title: ZipArchiveInputStream STORED-with-data-descriptor resynchronization relies on signature scanning of attacker-controlled content
description: readStoredEntry() buffers the current STORED entry (used when the entry uses a data descriptor and allowStoredEntriesWithDataDescriptor is enabled) by reading it into a ByteArrayOutputStream and scanning for the LFH/CFH/DD signatures. bufferContainsSignature() only inspects the first two bytes for the local/central header start and then confirms with a mix of LFH and CFH byte positions (buf[i]==LFH[0] && buf[i+1]==LFH[1] then either LFH[2]/LFH[3] or CFH[2]/CFH[3]); if a match is found the code computes readTooMuch = offset + lastRead - i - expectedDDLen, pushes the excess bytes back, writes the pre-signature prefix into the accumulator, and calls readDataDescriptor(). title: Expander relies on getCanonicalPath prefix matching for path-traversal containment (candidate, not confirmed)
description: Expander#expand(ArchiveEntrySupplier, EntryWriter, File) computes the target directory's canonical path, appends File.separatorChar if missing, and rejects entries whose resulting file canonical path does not start with that prefix. title: ZipArchiveInputStream STORED-with-data-descriptor entries are fully buffered into a ByteArrayInputStream (unbounded memory, potential OOM/DoS)
description: In ZipArchiveInputStream.readStored, when the current entry is STORED and uses a data descriptor, the code calls readStoredEntry() and only then serves data from lastStoredEntry (a ByteArrayInputStream). readStoredEntry() reads the whole entry into an in-memory buffer before returning, so the size of the allocation is controlled by the attacker-supplied archive (the entry's uncompressed/compressed size, i.e., the amount of stored data preceding the descriptor), not by the caller's read() length. An archive containing a large STORED entry with the data-descriptor bit set causes the entire entry to be buffered in memory regardless of how little the caller consumes, which can exhaust the heap on a constrained consumer. readStoredEntry() is also reachable from ZipFile.getInputStream for data-descriptor stored entries (per the ZipFile source searched), so both the streaming and seekable APIs can trigger a full-entry buffering step. This is a resource-consumption concern rather than memory corruption; the library provides getCompressedCount()/getUncompressedCount() statistics for callers to implement their own limits, but no built-in cap is applied here.

title: ZipArchiveInputStream.closeEntry() casts a long byte-count difference to int for pushback
description: In closeEntry(), after draining/skipping, the code computes 'final int diff = (int) (current.bytesReadFromStream - inB);' where bytesReadFromStream and inB are derived from long counters (bytesReadFromStream is a long incremented by stream reads; inB is from getBytesInflated(), which reconciles Inflater byte counts across 2^32 wraps). The comment asserts the value 'is at most a single read() operation and can't exceed the range of int', but this relies on the invariant that the difference never exceeds one buffer (BUFFER_SIZE). If, for a malformed or large ZIP64 entry, bytesReadFromStream exceeds inB by more than Integer.MAX_VALUE, the narrowing cast could produce an unexpected/negative diff, which then feeds pushback(buf.array(), buf.limit() - diff, diff) and additional draining logic. A negative or wrong diff would lead to an incorrect pushback length/offset (buf.limit()-diff larger than the buffer or a negative length) and could throw or corrupt stream positioning. This is a robustness/parsing-integrity candidate dependent on the size accounting invariants holding.

title: Unbounded heap allocation from ZIP header file-name/extra-field lengths (potential DoS)
description: ZipArchiveInputStream.getNextZipEntry() reads the local file header and obtains fileNameLen (from ZipShort.getValue) and extraLen directly from the untrusted archive bytes. It then unconditionally allocates byte arrays of those sizes (new byte[fileNameLen], new byte[extraLen]) and calls readFully on them. The lengths are 16-bit, so a single entry can force allocation of up to ~65535 bytes for the name plus ~65535 for extra data, with no validation against available stream data and no overall memory cap in this class. A crafted archive with many such entries, or with the class used repeatedly, can drive unbounded heap usage / memory exhaustion (denial of service). The security-reports.xml documents a related class of malicious-ZIP denial-of-service issues in this package. The length fields themselves are derived from attacker-controlled input, and no upper bound or limit is enforced before allocation.

title: Stored-entry data-descriptor signature scan may misparse entry boundaries and mislocate subsequent entries
description: In ZipArchiveInputStream, stored entries using a data descriptor are handled by readStoredEntry()/bufferContainsSignature(), which scans a buffer for LFH/CFH/DD signatures (comparing byte pairs) to decide where the entry data ends and the data descriptor begins. This is a robustness/parsing-boundary concern, not a demonstrated memory-safety or arbitrary-write bug.

title: ZipArchiveInputStream.readStoredEntry buffers a whole data-descriptor STORED entry into memory
description: For STORED entries that use a data descriptor, readStoredEntry() accumulates all entry bytes into a ByteArrayOutputStream (line 892) by looping on in.read into a buffer sized by ZipArchiveOutputStream.BUFFER_SIZE (lines 899-916) until a local-file-header, central-directory or data-descriptor signature is found. label: pro_max
title: Archive expansion path traversal bypass via symlink entries
description: Expander.expand() writes archive entries into targetDirectory using each entry's name. The containment check uses File.getCanonicalPath() computed BEFORE any entry is written and compares only prefix strings. An attacker who controls a malicious archive can place a symlink as one or more entries (a 'link' entry, e.g. a tar/zip symlink whose target points outside targetDirectory) ahead of a later entry whose name traverses through that symlink. Because the canonical-path check is performed at write time of each entry but the prior symlink entry may have already created a link inside targetDirectory pointing outside it, a subsequent entry whose path goes through the symlink resolves (canonically) to a location outside targetDirectory while the naive startsWith check can still pass if the entry name string begins with the target directory prefix. This is the classic zip-slip/arbitrary-file-write-via-symlink issue. The evidence shows: entry names come directly from the archive (supplier.getNextReadableEntry().getName()), the check uses getCanonicalPath().startsWith() (string-prefix), directory/symlink entries are written via mkdirs (which can be a pre-created symlink), and there is no check that an entry is not a symlink or that canonical path of the parent directory is still inside targetDirectory after earlier entries were written. Root cause: containment is validated via string prefix of canonical path of the constructed File, without re-verifying after earlier entries may have introduced symlinks, and without rejecting symlink/link entries.

label: flash_max
title: Attacker-controlled multipart boundary length is not bounded before use in MultipartStream (potential CPU/memory DoS)
description: MultipartStream's central constructor computes the delimiter array directly from the caller-supplied boundary byte array without any maximum-length check. It evaluates boundary.length in the array sizing (specifically new byte[boundary.length + BOUNDARY_PREFIX.length], the derived boundaryLength, and keepRegion = boundary.length), then copies the caller bytes. The same boundaryLength drives the inner comparison loop in findSeparator(), which is invoked from ItemInputStream construction (constructor at line 811 calls findSeparator()) and after every buffer refill in makeAvailable() (line 1010). When the buffer contains bytes that repeatedly match only the initial byte of the boundary (for example many CR bytes, since boundary[0] is CR after BOUNDARY_PREFIX), findByte returns positions that each trigger up to boundaryLength byte comparisons inside the for(match = 1; match < boundaryLength; match++) loop. A large boundary therefore multiplies the work done per buffered byte, and the full boundary string is materialized in a heap array whose size is derived from the attacker-controlled header value. This is the structural precondition underlying the historical boundary-length DoS class. Reachability/severity depend entirely on how FileUploadBase.getBoundary() (which parses the Content-Type header) and parseRequest() validate the boundary before constructing MultipartStream; those methods lie outside the source lines that were actually read, so exploitation is not established here.

label: flash_high
title: Predictable temporary file names in DiskFileItem.getTempFile enable local TOCTOU/symlink attacks when repository is shared
description: DiskFileItem stores large (>sizeThreshold) parts in a temp file whose name is derived from a static UUID (uid) and an incrementing AtomicInteger counter: format("upload_%s_%s.tmp", UID, getUniqueId()). The UID is per-classloader and not secret, and getUniqueId() returns a zero-padded, monotonically increasing decimal counter (00000000, 00000001, ...). When the configured repository is null, it falls back to the System property java.io.tmpdir. The file content is written via DeferredFileOutputStream to this path. A local attacker who can write to the temp directory can pre-create the same name (as a file or symlink) before the write, or swap it afterward, giving a write-through/link redirection (TOUTOC). The DiskFileItemFactory javadoc explicitly warns about this and mandates setRepository on a non-publicly-writable location, so the mitigation is documentation-level and the safe behavior is opt-in.

title: Per-part file size limit is bypassable by omitting the part Content-length; library defaults impose no size limit at all
description: In FileUploadBase.FileItemStreamImpl, the per-part fileSizeMax enforcement is split into two independent mechanisms: (a) a pre-check that only runs when the sender supplied a content length for that part — if (pContentLength != -1 && pContentLength > fileSizeMax) … throw FileSizeLimitExceededException — and (b) a LimitedInputStream wrapper that enforces the limit while the body is actually read. Mechanism (a) is therefore trivially skipped if pContentLength == -1 (no Content-length header on the part or an unknown length), and it is mechanism (b) that must catch such requests. Separately, both configurable limits default to -1, documented as "no limit" (getSizeMax/setSizeMax lines 156-221 for sizeMax, getFileSizeMax/setFileSizeMax lines 163-243 for fileSizeMax), and the request-level guard at lines 963-981 only installs a LimitedInputStream when sizeMax >= 0, while the constructor check requestSize != -1 && requestSize > sizeMax is likewise conditional. title: Default temporary-file repository combined with predictable file names in DiskFileItem

title: MultipartStream refill loop can spin without consuming input when the attacker-controlled boundary exceeds the internal buffer size
description: MultipartStream constructs its fixed working buffer from bufSize and sets keepRegion from the boundary length, without requiring the buffer to be at least as large as the boundary: `this.buffer = new byte[bufSize]; ... this.boundaryLength = boundary.length + BOUNDARY_PREFIX.length; this.keepRegion = this.boundary.length;` (MultipartStream.java:329-336). The boundary is taken verbatim from the client-supplied Content-type header (FileUploadBase.getBoundary, lines 419-435, which lower-cases parameter names, reads `boundary`, and byte-encodes it with no length limit; FileItemIteratorImpl passes it to the MultipartStream constructor). The delimiter search can only find a boundary that lies fully inside the buffer: findSeparator computes `maxpos = tail - boundaryLength` and immediately returns -1 when maxpos < head (MultipartStream.java:697-718). So with boundaryLength larger than bufSize, no separator is ever found. In ItemInputStream.makeAvailable (MultipartStream.java:983-1017) the code moves `pad` bytes, sets `tail = pad`, and loops `int bytesRead = input.read(buffer, tail, bufSize - tail);` with no cap on iterations and no check for a zero-length read. When the buffer fills up, `bufSize - tail` becomes 0 and `tail += bytesRead` adds nothing, findSeparator again returns -1, and available() returns `tail - head - pad` (MultipartStream.java:846-851) which is 0, so the `if (av > 0 || pos != -1)` exit is not taken. A zero-length InputStream.read is permitted to return 0 indefinitely, so the loop can keep executing without consuming stream data or advancing the buffer, i.e. CPU consumption while parsing. I could not confirm in the read source that a concrete transport (e.g. a servlet request stream) returns 0 for a zero-length read rather than -1, nor that the surrounding FileItemIteratorImpl rejects an over-long boundary, so exploitability is unverified. The observation consistent with the code is that the guard which forces a buffer big enough for the boundary is missing.

title: FilenameUtils.doNormalize leaves '..' segments that fall inside a UNC-style '//' prefix, so normalize() can return a path still containing parent-directory traversal
description:
Root cause: doNormalize() computes a prefix length via getPrefixLength(fileName) (line 361) and then runs its separator/segment-removal passes only at or after that prefix boundary: the adjoining-slash loop starts at i = prefix + 1 (line 385), the dot-slash loop at i = prefix + 1 (line 394), and the double-dot-slash loop at i = prefix + 2 (line 408). Any '.' or '..' segment occurring within [0, prefix) is therefore never inspected or removed.

For a leading double separator, getPrefixLength() treats '//' (or '\\') as a UNC prefix and returns the index of the next separator plus one (lines 671-679). For input such as "//../foo", the second separator at index 1 makes the code scan for the next '/'/'\\' from index 2; the next separator is at index 4, so prefix = 5. The ".." segment at indices 2-3 plus its trailing separator at index 4 all lie inside that prefix, so the triple-condition removal loop (which begins at prefix + 2, line 408) never evaluates them. The '..' survives normalization and normalize() returns a value still containing "..".

The Javadoc contract for this method states that "A double dot will cause that path segment and the one before to be removed" (line 305) and that if there is no parent segment to consume, null is returned (lines 306-307); the documented example "//server/../bar --> null" (line 324) shows that '..' immediately following a UNC prefix is intended to invalidate the result. The implementation does not satisfy that contract when the '..' is absorbed into the prefix, so a caller that relies on normalize() to produce a traversal-free path (a common defensive pattern when building file paths from external names) can still receive a path containing "..".

This is reported as a candidate weakness, not a confirmed exploit: the actual impact depends on the caller. Severity assessment would require knowing whether the normalized string is combined with a base directory and passed to a filesystem API, and on which platform (the double-separator prefix logic in getPrefixLength is applied for both '//' and '\\' regardless of the running OS, per lines 671-679 and the class comment at lines 623-625).

title: FilenameUtils.normalize treats Windows drive/UNC prefixes as absolute even on Unix, so a POSIX-callable path containing an embedded colon is not rejected as escaping
description: FilenameUtils.normalize(String) / normalize(String, boolean) delegate to doNormalize(char separator, boolean keepSeparator) (lines 196-198, 243-246, 290-292, 337-340). doNormalize first computes prefix = getPrefixLength(fileName) and returns null only if prefix < 0 (lines 361-364). getPrefixLength (lines 630-683) always recognizes Windows-style prefixes regardless of host OS: a leading ':' returns NOT_FOUND (639-640), but any first char followed by ':' where the char is A-Z (upper-cased) is treated as a drive prefix returning 2 or 3 (lines 658-665), and a leading pair of separators is treated as a UNC prefix (lines 671-679). The class javadoc explicitly notes both prefix styles are matched on every machine (lines 60-76). Consequently, inputs such as "C:/.." style names, or names whose first character is a letter/dot/other non-'/' followed by ':', acquire a non-zero prefix on a POSIX host, and the ".."-collapsing loop (lines 406-431) will remove the '..' segment relative to that prefix instead of returning null. The document/output is then returned with a Windows-flavored prefix rather than being flagged invalid. The javadoc contracts also promise null "if invalid" and that null bytes are removed (lines 193-194, 287-289); null-byte handling is actually enforced by failIfNullBytePresent(fileName) at line 355, so that specific old issue is guarded here. Root cause: OS-independent prefix detection in getPrefixLength combined with doNormalize trusting that prefix to bound '..' resolution. Preconditions to matter: an application on a non-Windows host must pass attacker-influenced text to FilenameUtils.normalize/normalizeNoEndSeparator and then use the returned value as a filesystem path; the library itself performs no file I/O here. Impact cannot be established from this repository alone because the caller/usage is absent. Counter-evidence: getPrefixLength was explicitly hardened by IO-483 (changes.xml lines 104-105; leading ':' rejected at lines 639-640, embedded invalid colon rejected at 666-669) and normalize is documented to return null for invalid names; FileUtils.resolveFile/canonical-path checks elsewhere in the project are the normal containment mechanism, and I did not read them. title: Hostname verification effectively disabled when disableCNCheck is enabled (SSLUtils.getHostnameVerifier)
description: SSLUtils.getHostnameVerifier() selects the HostnameVerifier returned for a TLS client. If TLSClientParameters.isDisableCNCheck() is true and no custom verifier and no 'use HttpsURLConnection default verifier' is configured, it returns new AllowAllHostnameVerifier(), which accepts any host. This means an application or configuration that sets disableCNCheck (directly or via configuration/jsse binding) silently disables server identity verification for HTTPS conduits, enabling man-in-the-middle interception. - engineVerify(byte[] signature) (lines 111-126) only enforces the safety rule inside a conditional: if (this.HMACOutputLengthSet && this.HMACOutputLength < getDigestLength()) { throw ... } else { byte[] completeResult = this.macAlgorithm.doFinal(); return MessageDigestAlgorithm.isEqual(completeResult, signature); }. label: flash_high
title: Unescaped interpolation in JCR-SQL2 query construction (sling-query resource JCR support)
description:
The sling-query JCR resource support builds JCR-SQL2 query text by direct string interpolation without any escaping or quoting of inputs.

In JcrOperator each operator handler embeds the caller-supplied key and value directly inside SQL2 literals:
- CONTAINS: String.format("s.[%s] LIKE '%%%s%%'", key, value) (line 26)
- ENDS_WITH: String.format("s.[%s] LIKE '%%%s'", key, value) (line 38)
- EQUALS: String.format("s.[%s] = '%s'", key, value) (line 44)
- NOT_EQUAL: String.format("s.[%s] != '%s'", key, value) (line 50)
- STARTS_WITH: String.format("s.[%s] LIKE '%s%%'", key, value) (line 56)
CONTAINS_WORD delegates to CONTAINS (line 32), and getSelectorOperator falls through to EQUALS for an unrecognized operator (line 74).

In JcrQueryBuilder the full statement is assembled by appending the primary type (findPrimaryType), then WHERE plus the assembled condition string; the condition string itself is built from ISDESCENDANTNODE('%s') with the raw rootPath (line 58), s.[sling:resourceType] = '%s' with the raw resourceType (line 112), and NAME(s) = '%s' with the raw resourceName (line 115), plus attribute conditions. None of these values are escaped or parameterized.

Root cause: query text is constructed with String.format/StringBuilder concatenation of externally derived key/value/type/name/path strings, so a value containing a single quote (and, in the operand-position key case, brackets) can break out of the intended literal/identifier context and alter the generated JCR-SQL2 statement. This is a classic SQL/query-injection pattern in query assembly.

Uncertainty: the read ranges show only the fragment and statement builders. Whether these values reach untrusted input (e.g., a user-supplied selector/attribute string) depends on callers that were not read, and any upstream escaping was not observed. The root path normally originates from the resolver rather than the request, which limits, but does not eliminate, the concern. This is reported as a candidate root cause, not a confirmed exploitable vulnerability.

The reader itself performs no sanitization of the entry name (no check for '../', absolute paths, or backslashes), so a malicious archive could contain entries whose names traverse out of the import target. Whether this is exploitable depends on how DefaultContentCreator.switchCurrentNode/createFileAndResourceNode resolve relative paths, which is implemented in a file outside the read spans. Reported as a potential Zip-slip/path-traversal surface, not a confirmed vulnerability.

title: XSLT stylesheet URL resolution and TransformerFactory execution driven by XML input in XmlReader
description: XmlReader parses XML whose content can specify an `xml-stylesheet` processing instruction with an `href` attribute. When the XML location is non-null, the parser resets the input and constructs an XslTransformerStream, which resolves `new URL(xmlLocation, xslHref)` and feeds the resulting URL as the XSL stylesheet source to `TransformerFactory.newInstance().newTemplates(xsl)`, then transforms the input XML with it. Because the `href` is taken verbatim from the XML document and resolved against the base location with no protocol/allow-list restriction, a crafted XML document can cause the server to open arbitrary URLs (file:, http:, jar:, etc.) and compile/execute attacker-supplied XSLT. The XML is untrusted where it derives from uploaded content/installation inputs. This is a candidate for SSRF and unsafe XSLT processing; it is not a confirmed vulnerability because the trust boundary (who can supply the XML) is unverified.

title: RedirectServlet writes a Location header from the sling:target repository property plus raw request selectors/extension/suffix/query string without isRedirectValid-style scheme/host validation
description: RedirectServlet.doGet reads the target from the resource ValueMap (sling:target) or adapts the sling:target child resource to String, then writes it into the response via setHeader("Location", targetPath). In the URL branch (isUrl(targetPath) true) the code appends request-derived selector/extension/suffix and the raw query string to the target and emits it as the redirect location. Unlike other Sling code paths that call AuthUtil.isRedirectValid (which rejects targets that are not absolute, contain control characters, or fail scheme/host checks), this servlet does not appear to invoke such a validator before setting the header; the target and appended request components are used verbatim. If a resource of type sling:redirect (with sling:target) can be created or modified by a lower-privileged author, or the property can hold an absolute/off-site URL, this yields an open-redirect / header-content injection primitive. Note the value is authored content, not a raw request parameter, so exploitation requires repository write permission on that resource.

title: SlingPostServlet HTTP redirect target derived from request parameter with only partial URI validation
description: In SlingPostServlet, the redirect target is taken directly from the request parameter SlingPostConstants.RP_REDIRECT_TO (getRedirectUrl, line 309). The code attempts to reject host-bearing targets by constructing a java.net.URI and checking getAuthority() (lines 312-317), and rejects unparsable URIs via URISyntaxException (lines 318-321). If the value passes, it is then reworked (star substitution, request-path prepending, create-suffix handling, lines 325-357) and finally passed to response.sendRedirect(encodedURL) in redirectIfNeeded (line 251). The validation is not a strict relative-path/scheme allow-list: it relies on URI authority presence, and the subsequent transformations can prepend request.getPathInfo() (line 347). This creates a candidate open-redirect / response-splitting concern because the final redirect destination is influenced by a client-supplied parameter and the sink (sendRedirect) is reached whenever the POST operation succeeds. Root cause: partial validation of the redirect parameter rather than enforcing a server-side allow-list of permitted redirect destinations.

title: getValidHref: colon-percent-encoding only applies after '?' and namespace mangling may alter scheme validation
description: XSSAPIImpl.getValidHref decodes the URL, unescapes XML entities, then percent-encodes only the characters ", ', >, <, ` and space. It then finds the first '?' at index qMarkIx and, only when qMarkIx > 0, replaces ':' with %3A in the substring starting at '?'. Finally it calls mangleNamespaces(encodedUrl) and only accepts the result if xssFilter.isValidHref(encodedUrl) returns true. Two aspects are worth review: (1) colons before the '?' (i.e., in the scheme/authority/path portion) are left unencoded, and (2) mangleNamespaces rewrites occurrences of the pattern /([^:/]+): into /_$1_ (e.g., a path segment like /foo:bar becomes /_foo_bar), which is a transformation performed on attacker-controlled input before it is handed to isValidHref. title: Static content loader decodes path after traversal-cleaning and passes it to classpath resource lookup
description: DefaultStaticContentLoader.findStaticResource() cleans the requested path, then for each configured path prefix builds the resource path with buildPath() and looks it up on the classpath via ClassLoaderUtil.getResource(). buildPath() performs URLDecoder.decode(resourcePath, encoding) *after* the prefix/name concatenation, i.e. after the path has already passed through cleanupPath()/lookup. A request such as /struts/.../%252e%252e/... can be double-encoded by the client; the decode performed here turns it into '../' only at the point where the resource name is handed to the class loader. The subsequent guard `if (resourceUrl.getFile().endsWith(pathEnding))` is a name-suffix check, not a canonical-path containment check, and it compares the resolved URL's file string against the still-encoded pathEnding, so it is fragile with respect to the decoded value. If the container/classloader resolves the decoded name outside the intended `static`/`template`/`org.apache.struts2.static` prefixes, arbitrary classpath resources (potentially including JARs/properties) could be served. Note also that the discovered InputStream is only assigned inside the try block and is used outside it, and the guard relies solely on string suffix matching.

label: flash_high
title: Hard-coded excluded patterns rely on full `matches()` semantics and may not cover dot/alternative separators used by OGNL
description:
ExcludedPatterns defines a set of hard-coded strings intended to be rejected by ParametersInterceptor. CLASS_ACCESS_PATTERN is `(.*\\.|^|.*|\\[('|\"))class(\\.|('|\")]|\\[).*` and the remaining entries are anchored namespace prefixes (`^dojo\..*`, `^struts\..*`, `^session\..*`, `^request\..*`, `^application\..*`, `^servlet(Request|Response)\..*`, `^parameters\..*`). ParametersInterceptor compiles each of these with Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE (ParametersInterceptor.java:502-507) and applies them with Matcher.matches() in isExcluded (ParametersInterceptor.java:451-462). Because the check is `matches()` (whole-string) rather than `find()`, a parameter name is only rejected if it matches a pattern in its entirety; the alternation inside CLASS_ACCESS_PATTERN ends with `.*`, so trailing content is tolerated, but any untrusted key whose shape differs from the enumerated namespaces (for example a different separator/case, or a class reference not using the literal `class` token in the supported brackets) would not be caught by the blacklist. The parameters interceptor additionally applies the whitelist regex ACCEPTED_PARAM_NAMES (ParametersInterceptor.java:146-159) and the whitelist short-circuits the blacklist only when acceptParams is non-empty (isAccepted, ParametersInterceptor.java:432-449); when acceptParams is empty the general acceptedPattern governs. Notably, if an operator configures `acceptParamNames`, isAccepted() returns true for anything matching those operator-supplied patterns and the action's default pattern is bypassed, while isExcluded still runs, so the effective guard is the conjunction described in acceptableName (ParametersInterceptor.java:416-422).

No concrete bypass string was verified in this review: establishing one would require running the compiled patterns or reading the OGNL member-access layer (SecurityMemberAccess/PropertiesJudge), which were not in the read spans. The candidate is that the blacklist is a pattern-matching, format-sensitive control whose correctness depends entirely on the exact separator/bracket encodings that OGNL accepts, and the read code does not itself demonstrate that all encodings are covered.

title: Action-name cleanup removes disallowed-character substrings instead of rejecting, potentially yielding unexpected derived action names
description:
DefaultActionMapper.parseNameAndNamespace sets mapping.name via cleanupActionName(name) (DefaultActionMapper.java:373-375), and cleanupActionName normally returns the raw action name when it matches the permissive allowedActionNames regex `[a-zA-Z0-9._!/\-]*` (DefaultActionMapper.java:122, 383-385). No end-to-end exploitation is shown: whether a cleaned name can select an unintended action requires the configuration/action lookup layer, which is outside the read span (getMapping is at DefaultActionMapper.java:252-267 and the read starts at 237).

title: ParametersInterceptor accepts parameter names by default via AcceptPatternsChecker whitelist while the class-instantiation guard remains a blacklist entry; unexamined excluded-pattern bypass surface
description: ParametersInterceptor.setParameters (lines 255-315) filters request parameter names with isAcceptableParameter -> acceptableName(name) = isWithinLengthLimit(name) && !isExcluded(name) && isAccepted(name) (lines 340-343, 412-418). isAccepted delegates to DefaultAcceptedPatternsChecker.ACCEPTED_PATTERNS = "\\w+((\\.\\w+)|(\\[\\d+\\])|(\\(\\d+\\))|(\\['(\\w|[\\u4e00-\\u9fa5])+'\\])|(\\('(\\w|[\\u4e00-\\u9fa5])+'\\)))*" (line 19), i.e. a positive whitelist that would not admit '#', '$', '@', '*' or '(' outside the '(\d+)' alternative. isExcluded delegates to DefaultExcludedPatternsChecker whose first entry is the well-known class-instantiation regex (line 19) intended to block "class.classLoader..."/"(class)" style injection. title: Recursive OGNL evaluation limited to MAX_RECURSION=1 in TextParseUtil/OgnlTextParser
description: TextParseUtil.translateVariables resolves ${...} and %{...} occurrences by invoking the injected TextParser (OgnlTextParser) with a max loop count. title: Request parameter binding in ParametersInterceptor exposes OGNL evaluation of attacker-controlled parameter names, guarded only by configurable regex whitelists/blacklists
description: ParametersInterceptor.doIntercept reads the request parameter map (attacker-controlled keys and values) and, for each accepted name, invokes newStack.setParameter(name, value), which compiles/evaluates the name as an OGNL expression against the action ValueStack. title: Action name sanitization removes matched substrings instead of rejecting unmatched names (DefaultActionMapper.cleanupActionName)
description: In DefaultActionMapper, action names extracted from the request URI are validated against the configurable pattern `allowedActionNames` (default `[a-zA-Z0-9._!/\-]*`). In parseNameAndNamespace the raw name is passed to cleanupActionName (line 374). cleanupActionName (lines 383-399): if the raw name matches the pattern it is returned unchanged; otherwise the code logs a warning and then, instead of rejecting the request, iteratively removes the substrings returned by `allowedActionNames.split(rawActionName)` from the raw name and returns that transformed value. Because the sanitization is a deletion of matched chunks rather than a rejection, characters outside the allowed pattern are dropped while surrounding characters are preserved, so a single untrusted URI segment can be transformed into a different (possibly valid) action name. The transformed name is then set on the ActionMapping and used for action resolution. Reachability from untrusted input is plausible: the URI comes from RequestUtils.getUri(request) in getMapping (line 254) and flows through parseNameAndNamespace to cleanupActionName (line 374). This is flagged as a candidate for review of the sanitization logic; I could not verify with the available tools whether a crafted input can reliably produce an attacker-chosen pre-existing action name, nor whether the derived mapping is later used for security-sensitive dispatch.

title: XSLTResult honors request parameter "xslt.location" to select the stylesheet, overriding the configured path
description: In XSLTResult.execute the configured location is passed to getTemplates(location) (line 365). Inside getTemplates the value is immediately replaced by ServletActionContext.getRequest().getParameter("xslt.location") whenever that parameter is non-null (lines 452-455), before the path is resolved through the servlet context (line 464) and compiled into a TransformerFactory template (lines 474-477). Nothing in the read span gates this on a configuration flag, and there is no allowlist, extension check, or normalization of the value. The template is then applied to an XML serialization of the action through transformer.transform (line 416), so the selected stylesheet controls what is emitted to the response. Preconditions: an action/result is configured with type="xslt" so this Result executes; the attacker can supply the "xslt.location" request parameter. title: DefaultActionMapper 'action:' prefix may allow cross-action/method invocation from request parameters
description: DefaultActionMapper registers an 'action:' prefix handler (ParameterAction) that, when `allowActionPrefix` is true, takes the remainder of the parameter key as the action name. title: XMLReaderUtils pool resize: setPoolSize() races with concurrent acquire/release and is called (with unvalidated size) from the acquire wait loop
description: setPoolSize(int) (lines 470-501) replaces the static SAX_PARSERS and DOM_BUILDERS queues with new ArrayBlockingQueue instances while holding only a write lock on the pool mutex, and it stores POOL_SIZE = poolSize at the very end after the queues have already been swapped. acquireSAXParser() (lines 410-437) and acquireDOMBuilder() (lines 347-374) poll the queue under a read lock, and after ~3000 iterations (a timer-based heuristic, not an exact count) call setPoolSize(POOL_SIZE) themselves (lines 366 and 429), i.e. a failing acquirer can trigger a pool replacement while other threads are mid-acquire/release. An in-flight parser/builder held by another thread will be offered back by releaseParser()/releaseDOMBuilder() (lines 381-399, 444-462) into a queue that may already have been replaced, producing the logged 'not taken back into pool' condition and silently discarding parsers. Additionally the size passed in is used directly to size the ArrayBlockingQueue ('new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(poolSize)'), so a zero/negative or otherwise out-of-range value supplied by an application embedding Tika (e.g. via XMLReaderUtils.setPoolSize) would throw or starve the pool; the public setter performs no range validation. title: Archive entry names used directly to build output paths in Zips.unzip (potential Zip Slip / path traversal)
description: Both `org.apache.openejb.arquillian.common.Zips.unzip` (arquillian/arquillian-tomee-common) and `org.apache.openejb.loader.Zips.unzip` (container/openejb-loader) iterate a ZipInputStream and construct the destination with `new File(destination, entry.getName())` (arquillian Zips.java line 55, loader Zips.java line 61) without canonicalizing the result and without rejecting entries whose names contain `..` or absolute path components. title: Zip Slip: Zips.unzip joins raw ZIP entry names onto the destination directory without containment check

title: Unquoted argument fallback in Shell.getRawCommandLine can inject shell metacharacters when quoting is disabled
description: In Shell.getRawCommandLine, when isQuotedArgumentsEnabled() is false, each argument is appended to the command StringBuilder with the plain statement `sb.append( arguments[i] );` (line 171) instead of being passed through StringUtils.quoteAndEscape (the quoted branch at line 167). The resulting single string is returned as a one-element list (lines 175-177) and, via getShellCommandLine (lines 266-285), is prefixed with the shell command and shell args. For BourneShell the command string is executed by /bin/sh via the `-c` argument (BourneShell.java:92 `shellArgs.add( "-c" );` and 105-113). Therefore any argument content containing shell metacharacters (e.g. ;, |, &, $(), backticks) is interpreted by the shell rather than treated as a literal argument, i.e. command injection through argument values. Root cause: the unquoted branch performs no escaping/quoting before concatenation into a shell-interpreted command line. Preconditions: a caller must invoke setQuotedArgumentsEnabled(false) (default is true per field initialization at Shell.java:49) and must pass attacker-influenced argument strings. Counter-evidence/limits: quoting is enabled by default, so a plain out-of-the-box caller is not affected; the risk materializes only for callers that deliberately disable argument quoting. title: Possible path traversal in archive extraction via FileUtils.resolveFile with unsanitized entry names
description: Expand.expandFile reads zip entry names and passes them to extractFile, which calls FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName) and then writes extracted content to that path via FileOutputStream, creating parent directories with mkdirs(). resolveFile (FileUtils.java:1308-1377) base-resolves relative names against baseFile and calls getCanonicalFile(), which defeats plain '..' and '.' traversal and collapses duplicate separators in the relative branch. This is reported as a candidate: confirming an actual overwrite requires the untrusted archive to be attacker-influenced and knowledge of the caller's model of trust.

title: DocumentBuilderFactory in DocumentUtil.getDocument is created without XXE hardening and parses from an arbitrary URL
description: DocumentUtil.getDocument(URL, ...) creates a DocumentBuilderFactory with only setValidating/setNamespaceAware/setSchema, then parses the content obtained from location.openConnection().getInputStream(). No XMLConstants.ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD / ACCESS_EXTERNAL_SCHEMA attributes, no FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, and no disallow-doctype-decl / external-entity features are set on the factory or the resulting DocumentBuilder. description: The ESI IncludeElement takes the src attribute (and alt attribute) directly from the page being rendered and passes it to Driver.render, which fetches it over HTTP/HTTPS. title: JWTDecoder does not bind the verification algorithm to the caller-selected verifier and does not reject alg=none when a verifier is supplied (algorithm confusion at the decode boundary)

label: flash_high
title: Signature verification skipped for any JWT written as "header.payload." (verification decision based on segment count, not algorithm)
description:
Root cause: the decoder treats a two-segment token as unsecured regardless of the header 'alg' value, and the private decode() skips verification whenever parts.length != 3.

Flow: JWTDecoder.decode(String, Verifier...) (lines 60-82) parses the header and then, for a token whose 'alg' is not none, selects a verifier via canVerify() and calls the private decode(). getParts() (lines 174-182) splits on '.' and returns the parts when parts.length == 3 OR (parts.length == 2 && encodedJWT.endsWith(".")). Because Java's String.split removes trailing empty tokens, the token "<header>.<payload>." yields a two-element array. In the private decode() (lines 143-172), 'message' is computed from the last '.' (line 144-146), the MissingVerifierException check (line 149) and the whole verification block (lines 153-157) both require parts.length == 3, so for a two-segment token the payload is deserialized at line 159 and returned at line 171 with no call to verifier.verify().

Consequence: an attacker who can make the application decode an attacker-supplied JWT can submit a token with header {"alg":"RS256"} (or HS256/HMAC/any algorithm supported by a configured verifier), an arbitrary payload, and an empty third segment, and the library returns the claims as valid without ever checking a signature. Note that this does not even require a verifier that matches the algorithm: if the verifier loop finds no match, 'verifier' stays null and no MissingVerifierException is raised because that check also requires three parts.

The same code shape is the legitimate encoding of an unsecured token (UnsecuredSigner.sign returns an empty byte array, JWTEncoder adds the base64 of it and joins parts -> "h.p."), so the format is attacker-reachable and indistinguishable from a real unsecured token after the fact.

title: Unsecured ("alg":"none") JWT accepted even when verifiers are supplied (unsecured guard bypassed by the same segment-count logic)

label: flash_high
title: Missing "alg" header leads to NullPointerException inside Verifier.canVerify()
description: Header.algorithm is the single field mapped from the 'alg' property (Header.java:33-34); if the attacker omits 'alg' from the JOSE header JSON, Jackson leaves the enum field null (no default and no @JsonProperty required=true). label: flash_high
title: HMAC signature compared with Arrays.equals (non-constant-time comparison)
description: HMACVerifier.verify computes the expected MAC and compares it with the received signature using Arrays.equals (HMACVerifier.java:76-80). Arrays.equals short-circuits at the first differing byte, so the comparison time depends on the number of matching leading bytes. This is the classic non-constant-time MAC comparison pattern; the recommended form is java.security.MessageDigest.isEqual (or an equivalent constant-time compare). Reported as a low-confidence/informational candidate: exploiting a byte-by-byte timing difference over a network against an HMAC whose expected value is derived from a secret is generally considered impractical here (the attacker cannot choose the expected value and would need to recover the MAC byte-by-byte through many measurements), and no measurement was performed.

label: flash_max
title: Unsigned JWT (alg=none) accepted even when verifiers are supplied
description: In JWTDecoder, both decode overloads short-circuit to returning the payload when header.algorithm == Algorithm.none, the token has exactly two parts, and either no varargs verifiers (line 69) or an empty verifier map (line 119) are present. The unsecured branch deserializes parts[1] and returns it as a JWT. Because the unsecured check is placed BEFORE the verifier lookup/verification logic (decode(encodedJWT, header, parts, verifier) at lines 81/132), the algorithm reported in the attacker-controlled header controls whether signature verification runs at all. A token of the form base64({"alg":"none"}).base64(payload). (note the trailing dot, which is what makes getParts() accept a 2-element array per lines 174-182) is returned unverified. label: flash_max
title: Signature verification result stored but algorithm not re-bound to verifier in varargs decode loop
description: In decode(String, Verifier...) the loop at lines 74-79 iterates all verifiers and, for each one that reports canVerify(header.algorithm) == true, assigns verifier = v. title: Malformed JWT input can trigger unchecked NullPointerException / ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
description: getParts(String) splits on '.' and accepts the result when parts.length == 3 or (length == 2 && endsWith('.')). decode then unconditionally indexes parts[0] (line 66/117) and parts[1] (line 70/120, 159) and computes encodedJWT.lastIndexOf('.') title: Signed message is recomputed with lastIndexOf('.') while the signature is taken from parts[2], so the verified byte range is not cross-checked against the parsed segments
description: getParts (lines 174-182) accepts a token only as 'splits into exactly 3 parts' or '2 parts while the raw string ends with .'. title: HMAC key strength is not validated, unlike RSA modulus length which is enforced

title: Acceptance of 'none' algorithm JWT without authentication when no verifiers are supplied

An attacker who can supply input to a caller that invokes decode with an empty verifier set can forge arbitrary claims (issuer, subject, role/privilige claims via the generic claims map) by simply base64url-encoding a header with alg=none and an arbitrary payload. This is the classic 'alg:none' algorithm-confusion vulnerability. The root cause is the unconditional acceptance of the none algorithm tied to verifiers.length == 0 / verifiers.isEmpty().

title: Non-constant-time HMAC signature comparison using Arrays.equals
description: HMACVerifier.verify computes the expected MAC and compares it to the attacker-supplied signature with java.util.Arrays.equals. title: HMAC secret accepted with no minimum-length validation
description: HMACSigner and HMACVerifier accept any non-null string as the HMAC secret and convert it to bytes without enforcing a minimum entropy/length. label: pro_max
title: Algorithm 'none' accepted when decoding without a verifier (algorithm confusion risk)
description: JWTDecoder.decode(String, Verifier...), the no-verifier overload, and the Map overload explicitly return a deserialized JWT payload when the header algorithm equals Algorithm.none and there are only two token segments (header.payload) and no verifiers were supplied. An attacker who controls the token can craft an unsigned JWT with header alg=none that will be fully trusted as long as the application invokes decode() without any Verifier. Additionally, in the surrounding decode path the verifier is chosen solely by the attacker-controlled header 'alg' value (canVerify on header.algorithm), so a token forged with a different algorithm than the application expects will be validated against whatever verifier matches that algorithm. Whether this is exploitable depends on caller configuration: the no-verifier path is guarded by the verifiers.length == 0 / isEmpty() checks, and a 3-part token without a matching verifier throws MissingVerifierException. This is the well-known 'alg:none' / algorithm-confusion JWT weakness, reported as a candidate rather than a confirmed vulnerability because the safe usage pattern (always supplying a verifier) is supported and cannot be verified from this codebase.

label: pro_max
title: Verifier selection trusts attacker-controlled header 'alg' value
description: In JWTDecoder.decode(String, Verifier...), the verifier is matched by testing each supplied verifier's canVerify(header.algorithm), where header.algorithm is deserialized from the attacker-controlled JWT header. Similarly the Map overload looks up the verifier by a kid key derived from the attacker-controlled header and then re-checks canVerify. There is no independent expectation of which algorithm should be used; the token's own alg claim dictates which cryptographic verification path is trusted. Combined with an HMAC secret configured as an RSA verifier (or vice versa), this enables the classic algorithm-confusion attack (e.g., RS/HS confusion) if an application shares a key between algorithm families. The library itself cannot detect this because the verifier type encodes the algorithm family. Reported as a candidate; exploitability depends entirely on how verifiers and keys are configured by callers.

title: Java native deserialization of remote transport data in TransportFormat.readSerializableFrom (SERIALIZED branch)
description: TransportFormat.readSerializableFrom dispatches on the transport format; for the SERIALIZED case it wraps the input stream in `new ObjectInputStream(bufferedInput)` and calls `in.readObject()`, returning the result after a generic cast to `Serializable` at the end of the method. There is no class allow/deny filtering, no ObjectInputFilter, and no authentication/binding of the stream to a trusted producer inside this method. Per CollectorServer (seen in the read span), the collect server periodically connects out to the configured monitored-application URLs to obtain this stream, hence the bytes are supplied by a remote network peer rather than local trusted code. A peer that controls the response body (malicious/compromised monitored app, substituted URL, or on-path attacker) can therefore present an arbitrary serialized object graph to a native Java deserialization call, which is the classic gadget-chain code-execution surface. This is reported as a candidate, not a confirmed vulnerability: no gadget chain, no reachable call site outside the collector's own pull loop, and no effective upstream guard were verified in the read spans.

title: CollectorServlet POST adds a caller-controlled application URL (http/https only) that is later fetched and deserialized without authentication
description:
CollectorServlet.doPost reads 'appName' and 'appUrls' straight from the request and, after only a prefix check that appUrls starts with 'http://' or 'https://', calls collectorController.addCollectorApplication(appName, appUrls). The only access control is isAddressNotAllowed(req), which returns false whenever 'allowedAddrPattern' is null (i.e. whenever no allowed-addr-pattern parameter is configured, which is the default). CollectorController.addCollectorApplication then parses the URLs and forwards them to collectorServer.addCollectorApplication; the collector server stores them and RemoteCollector later issues HTTP GETs to those URLs, taking the response body and passing it to TransportFormat.readSerializableFrom. In the SERIALIZED format that method wraps the response in a java.io.ObjectInputStream and calls readObject(); in the XML format it builds an XStream instance and calls fromXML. As a result, anyone able to reach the collector servlet (no authentication is visible in the read code) can register a URL pointing at a server they control and have the collector server deserialize attacker-supplied data, which is the classic gadget-chain / external-entity exposure surface. Under the read code the data is trusted only so far as the operator ensures every polled URL is trusted; the default configuration does not enforce that.

Note: transport format choice, XStream version (older, from pom.xml), and whether the collector servlet is deployed behind additional authentication are outside the read spans, so this is reported as a candidate, not a confirmed vulnerability.

title: Apache Commons Digester in CcmParser.createParse rejects no XML external entities (potential XXE on CCM report XML)
description: CcmParser.parseCCMXmlFile builds an org.apache.commons.digester.Digester and calls digester.parse(ccmXmlFile) on the report InputStream. If any is set to false, the corresponding expression falls through to super.transform and is not routed through Checker at all. Additionally, in Checker the terminal fallbacks execute the raw operation via fakeCallSite(...).call/...callStatic/...callConstructor (e.g., lines 152-159, 182-190, 193-202) when chain.hasNext() is false, i.e., when no interceptor is registered. Thus a misconfiguration (flag turned off, or no interceptor registered) silently disables enforcement and executes the underlying call rather than failing closed.

title: checkedCast probes interface methods and constructors while discarding return values, relying on interceptor side effects
description: checkedCast, when coercing an object into an interface, enumerates the interface's methods and invokes each one on the target object with default-valued arguments (lines 546-566), explicitly ignoring the return value; similarly for coercing collections/maps to concrete types it invokes the constructor path (lines 567-589). These probe invocations run the target's methods/constructors for the purpose of letting interceptors reject them. If the supplied interceptor does not throw on these probes, the probe methods themselves execute with side effects. The correctness of enforcement depends entirely on the interceptor policy, not on the transformation.

label: flash_max
title: Checker falls through to executing the raw operation when no interceptor is registered (no default deny)
description: All Checker.checked* entry points build an invoker chain and, when the chain has no next interceptor, directly perform the underlying Groovy operation rather than denying it: checkedCall calls fakeCallSite(method).call(receiver,args) (line 157), checkedStaticCall calls fakeCallSite(method).callStatic((Class)receiver,args) (line 188), checkedConstructor calls fakeCallSite("<init>").callConstructor((Class)receiver,args) (line 200), checkedGetProperty/checkedSetProperty/checkedGetAttribute/checkedSetAttribute call ScriptBytecodeAdapter.getProperty/setProperty/getField/setField directly (lines 290, 347, 372, 406), and checkedGetArray/checkedSetArray call the fake "getAt"/"putAt" call sites (lines 422, 447). The comment at lines 149-151 explains that this fake-call-site path is the intended fallback. The safety of the whole design therefore rests entirely on the embedder having registered a strict interceptor in the current thread before executing the script; if registration is forgotten, misses a specific callback, or the interceptor only overrides a subset of the on* methods (GroovyInterceptor's defaults at lines 22-141 all forward the call unchanged), the sandboxed operation proceeds with no denial anywhere in the read code. This is a fail-open design rather than a defense-in-depth default-deny. Precondition is a host that invokes Checker without a fully restrictive interceptor; no such host configuration is present in the read set, so this is a design observation about the enforcement layer, not a demonstrated bypass.

title: Interception is AST-rewriting only; unrewritten constructs and compiler-materialised calls escape checking
description: Enforcement happens by rewriting expressions in innerTransform. Constructs the transformer deliberately leaves alone are executed unchecked: instanceof (SandboxTransformer.java lines 538-539), logical operators (lines 541-542), FieldExpression on the LHS of an assignment (lines 512-516, with the comment that it is 'not sure how we can intercept this, so skipping this for now'), and special constructor calls this(...)/super(...) Additionally whole categories only occur when their boolean flag is enabled (interceptMethodCall, interceptConstructor, interceptProperty, interceptArray, interceptAttribute at lines 105-124); if a flag is turned off each corresponding `if (... && interceptXxx)` is skipped and super.transform(exp) is used, leaving the operation unchecked. Because the checks are attached to specific AST node types at the CANONICALIZATION phase (constructor at line 127), anything Groovy or an AST transformation generates after this phase, or any expression form not handled in innerTransform, is not routed through Checker. Runtime property/method lookup that bypasses the rewritten AST shape (e.g. MetaClass-driven dispatch, closures, dynamic construction) therefore has no Checker boundary to cross; this is a structural property of the design visible in the read source.

description: To decide whether `foo` is a local variable or an implicit-this property access, the transformer relies on a compile-time variable-scope tracker and a `visitingClosureBody` flag. title: super(...) constructor interception is chained through onSuperConstructor with no enforce in Checker
description: For classes whose superclass is not in TRIVIAL_CONSTRUCTORS (lines 151-162), processConstructors rewrites each constructor to (a) generate an auxiliary private constructor whose first statement calls the real super via scwArgs (lines 208-229) and (b) emit checkedSuperConstructor(superClass, args) before delegating with this(...) Checker.checkedSuperConstructor (lines 234-244) runs a VarArgInvokerChain and calls chain.next().onSuperConstructor(this, superClass, args) but ignores the result and unconditionally returns a new SuperConstructorWrapper(args); if the chain is empty it does nothing at all (no else branch, unlike checkedCall). GroovyInterceptor.onSuperConstructor (lines 55-57) by default forwards to onNewInstance, but a custom interceptor that expects to validate or veto the super construction receives a void-returning hook whose only veto is throwing. This is a design/robustness concern around the SECURITY-582 handling; the read source does not show a working bypass.

title: Interceptor registration is per-thread and inherited; a missing/mis-scoped registration silently disables all checks
description: GroovyInterceptor.register() adds the interceptor to threadInterceptors.get() for the current thread (lines 194-196), and the class javadoc states the list is 'maintained per thread' (line 14). title: checkedCast notifies interceptors but ignores their decisions before performing the real coercion
description: Checker.checkedCast is the interception point for cast expressions and for implicit coercion of Collection/Map right-hand sides. label: flash_max
title: Per-thread interceptor registry lifecycle: non-LIFO unregister with no scoped helper for a security-relevant chain
description: GroovyInterceptor keeps interceptors in a per-thread CopyOnWriteArrayList and exposes them via an unmodifiable view. register() appends; unregister() removes by equals(). Because removal uses List.remove(Object) semantics, a sandbox that re-registers the same instance or unregisters in a non-LIFO order can silently drop a different interceptor layer than intended, since the list is order-sensitive and each element is consulted in turn. There is no scoped/try-finally registration helper in this repository, so an exception thrown during script evaluation combined with manual unregister() calls can leave the thread's interceptor list unexpected; Checker would then dispatch script calls to a reduced (or empty) chain, in which case each invoker chain's fallback executes the real operation.
