title: Update-center JSON signature verification: weak/downgradable certificate and digest handling in JSONSignatureValidator (candidate, unverified)
description:
In core/src/main/java/jenkins/util/JSONSignatureValidator.java, verifySignature(JSONObject o) performs update-site metadata signature verification. Within the read span (lines 1-120) the following behaviors are visible and are worth flagging as candidates:

- Lines 56-60: the 'signature' block is fetched, and when absent/null the method returns an error ('No signature block found'). When present, the block is removed from the object before canonicalization. This is the intended anti-append design.

- Lines 94-109 (comment block plus code): the in-source comment explicitly states that the legacy 'digest'/'signature' pair must be ignored because accepting it 'creates a vulnerability that allows the attacker to inject a fragment at the end of the json.' The code canonicalizes the object (with the signature block removed) into a TeeOutputStream feeding both a SHA1 DigestOutputStream and a SignatureOutputStream. Whether the *provided* legacy 'digest' field is truly never consulted depends on lines beyond 120 (the compare logic), which were not read.

- Lines 65-79: certificates are parsed from the JSON array, each is passed through c.checkValidity(), but both CertificateExpiredException and CertificateNotYetValidException are caught and converted only to a FormValidation warning (warning = FormValidation.warning(...)); verification then continues. Certificate validity is therefore not a hard gate in the visible code.

- Lines 62-91: all parsed certificates are collected, CertificateUtil.validatePath(certs, loadTrustAnchors(cf)) is invoked for path validation, but the RSA signature is initialized with only the first certificate (sig.initVerify(certs.get(0))) at line 90. Only an explicit certs.isEmpty() guard at line 87 prevents an index error; the read span does not show the loadTrustAnchors implementation (lines beyond 120), so the trust-root source and whether an attacker-supplied CA can satisfy the anchor set cannot be evaluated.

- Lines 82, 86: SHA1 and SHA1withRSA are used for the digest and signature algorithm.

- Lines 111-120: the 'correct_digest' value is read via optString and compared case-insensitively against the recomputed SHA1 digest; the visible portion shows a mismatch produces a message but the pass/fail effect of that branch completes after line 120, so the enforcement outcome is not observable in the read span.

Net: within the read window, certificate-validity failures are non-fatal warnings rather than rejections, only the first certificate is used for signature verification, and the digest comparison result is not shown to abort verification. Combined with the method comment acknowledging that mishandling the legacy digest/signature pair permits trailing-fragment injection, this is a plausible metadata-integrity weakness for update-center/plugin-download metadata. It is reported as a candidate only: the caller side, the trust-anchor implementation, and the final comparison/return logic were not read, so neither runtime reachability nor actual bypass is established.

title: CLICommand.main performs an authorization check using transport-level Authentication before CLI/authenticator identity is established
description: In CLICommand.main (core/src/main/java/hudson/cli/CLICommand.java), the security context is primed with the transport-provided Authentication (line 264: sc.setAuthentication(getTransportAuthentication())), then an initial Jenkins.READ check is executed at line 268 before args4j parses arguments and before the CliAuthenticator/loadStoredAuthentication flow establishes the effective identity (lines 269-273). The first check is therefore evaluated against the identity supplied by the CLI transport (for HTTP-tunneled CLI, the HTTP session authentication; for SSH CLI, the SSH user), not against the command-line credentials the user may have supplied via --username/--password. title: Crumb validation depends on MD5-based DefaultCrumbIssuer and returns null issueCrumb for non-HttpServletRequest
description: DefaultCrumbIssuer constructs its MessageDigest as MD5 and issues crumbs by hashing the authenticated principal name and client IP together with a salt. validateCrumb compares values via MessageDigest.isEqual (constant-time). The crumb is only a function of (user name, client IP when not excluded, salt); when 'excludeClientIPFromCrumb' is enabled the crumb no longer binds to the client address, so any value that leaks or can be recomputed for the target user (with a known salt) is reusable from other hosts. Additionally, issueCrumb returns null when the request is not an HttpServletRequest and the digest was unavailable (readResolve leaves md null on NoSuchAlgorithmException), and validateCrumb then returns false, i.e. failures are closed rather than open. This is a weakness/design observation about the default crumb algorithm rather than a demonstrated bypass; no exploitation path is verified in source.

title: Client IP used in crumb taken from untrusted X-Forwarded-For header
description: DefaultCrumbIssuer.getClientIP reads the X-Forwarded-For request header and, when present, splits it on comma and uses the first element as the client IP incorporated into the crumb. title: CSRF crumb derived from spoofable client IP / static salt, validation only on POST
description: DefaultCrumbIssuer.issueCrumb builds the crumb input from the authenticated principal name, a ';' separator, an optional client IP, and finally a descriptor-level salt; the digest is MD5 over that buffer with the salt appended (lines 76-87). CrumbFilter applies the crumb check only to method "POST" (line 71) and returns early for other methods (line 104-106), accepting the crumb from a header or from a request parameter (extractCrumbFromRequest lines 109-120). Any endpoint that performs a state change and is reachable through a non-POST method, or that is exempted through the CrumbExclusion extension point, gets no crumb enforcement. The practical strength of the token therefore rests on a static salt plus principal name plus a spoofable IP, which is weaker than a per-session random token.

title: Credential-submission flow validates CSRF crumb only after MultipartFormDataParser has consumed the request
description: SubversionSCM.DescriptorImpl.doPostCredential performs its authorization check first (Hudson.getInstance().checkPermission(Item.CONFIGURE), line 2249) and then constructs MultipartFormDataParser from the request (line 2251). title: Whitelist protocol check uses naive prefix match on resolved URL, allowing non-whitelisted / crafted schemes to pass
description:
Whitelist.testValidProtocol (safety/Whitelist.java lines 514-541) resolves the attribute value via Element.absUrl, and if that fails, falls back to the raw attribute value (line 518-519). It then lowercases the value and checks `value.toLowerCase().startsWith(prot)` where prot is e.g. "http:" (lines 534-538). This is a simple string-prefix test, not a scheme comparison. title: URL attribute whitelist uses prefix matching with raw fallback (potential sanitizer bypass)
description: Whitelist.testValidProtocol resolves the attribute value to an absolute URL via el.absUrl(attr.getKey()); if that yields an empty string it falls back to the raw attribute value ('if it could not be made abs, run as-is to allow custom unknown protocols'). label: flash_high
title: Server-side fetch of attacker-influenced stylesheet URL via CSS @import (embedStyleSheets)
description: When the policy enables embedding stylesheets, the CSS handler accepts the URI supplied in an attacker-controlled @import rule and only checks it against the policy's common regexps offsiteURL/onsiteURL and against being an absolute reference, then queues it for fetching. ExternalCssScanner consumes that queue and performs a server-side HTTP GET to the URI with size and timeout limits. Because the decision is delegated entirely to policy regexps (which I could not read), an application using a permissive policy (e.g. offsiteURL/onsiteURL broad or matching any http(s) host) could cause the server to issue requests to attacker-chosen hosts, including internal/loopback/link-local targets. This is reported as a candidate SSRF/outbound-request concern; reachability depends on embedStyleSheets being enabled and on the actual regexp contents. Relevant sinks and flow: CssHandler.importStyle constructs the URI, runs the regexps, and adds it to importedStyleSheets; ExternalCssScanner.parseImportedStylesheets then builds a GetMethod with the URI and executes it. The transport itself (commons-httpclient) is used directly without an allowlist.

title: SAX filter treats any tag whose name is a suffix of "style" as a CSS/style element
description: MagicSAXFilter.startElement computes `boolean isStyle = "style".endsWith(element.localpart)`. This is true not only for tag name "style" but for any localpart that is a non-empty suffix of the string "style" (e.g. "tyle", "yle", "le", "e"). When true, the filter pushes Ops.CSS, buffers the element's character content into cssContent, and on endElement re-emits the element with the scanned CSS content as its children (super.startElement(element, cssAttributes) then super.characters of the cleaned CSS). This means tags whose name the policy otherwise trims/keeps are instead routed through the CSS validator and re-emitted with attacker-influenced content, a behavior inconsistent with the intended style-only special-casing. The practical security impact (e.g., whether crafted content can escape CSS validation) depends on the CssScanner behavior and serialization, which were not read.

title: Password credentials stored with a fast single-iteration SHA-256 and non-CSPRNG salt
description: Credential.forPassword(int) generates a 16-byte random salt and stores the digest of SHA-256 over (salt || UTF-8 password), with DIGEST_ALGO = SHA-256 used directly. This is a fast-hash, no-key-stretching scheme: a single SHA-256 invocation is evaluated per candidate password, so offline brute-force/dictionary attacks against a leaked auth store are cheap compared to PBKDF2/bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2 with an iteration/work factor. The per-user salt prevents rainbow-table reuse and identical-hash reuse, and Credential.byteEquals performs a length-checked, non-early-exit comparison of the stored and computed digest, so an online timing oracle against the comparison is largely mitigated. The root issue is the absence of a key-derivation work factor in the reviewed code, not the presence of a logic bug. A secondary point in the same code: randomSalt() fills the salt using ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextBytes(salt). java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom is not a cryptographically secure generator; 16 bytes drawn from it are not a predictable constant, but salt uniqueness/unpredictability may be weaker than a SecureRandom-backed salt would provide. Note the digest field is also used for the legacy/unsupported password case, which appears to compare only the literal 'unsupported' value, a separate and not security-relevant path. These are storage-strength leads; no runtime exploitation is demonstrated or claimed.

title: SpEL expression parsing of request-derived property names in MapDataBinder
description: MapDataBinder.MapPropertyAccessor.setPropertyValue(String propertyName, Object value) feeds the propertyName directly into a Spring SpEL expression parser (PARSER.parseExpression(propertyName)) and then evaluates it with expression.setValue(context, value). propertyName originates from untrusted request parameter names bound through the parent WebDataBinder. title: JSON Patch 'path' from request body is compiled into a SpEL expression without validation or escaping (expression injection)
description:

Each PatchOperation constructor stores the raw path and immediately builds an expression from it (PatchOperation.java lines 61-67: this.path = path; ... this.spelExpression = pathToExpression(path);). title: RegexRequestMatcher appends the raw query string before matching, so anchored regex patterns can fail to match protected request paths

label: flash_high
title: RegexRequestMatcher compiles patterns without Pattern.DOTALL, allowing '.*' path patterns to be bypassed with encoded newline in the request URL
description:
RegexRequestMatcher is a security-sensitive RequestMatcher used (directly or indirectly) to decide whether an incoming request is covered by a security rule. In the constructor (lines 66-75) the supplied pattern is compiled with only the optional Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE flag; there is no Pattern.DOTALL (or equivalent inline flag) and a repository-wide search for "DOTALL" returned zero matches. In matches(HttpServletRequest) the matcher builds the URL from request.getServletPath() + request.getPathInfo() + ('?' + queryString) (lines 91-106) and then evaluates it with pattern.matcher(url).matches() (line 113), i.e. a full-string match against that concatenated value.

Under standard Java regex semantics the '.' metacharacter does not match line terminators unless DOTALL is set. Consequently a pattern written in the common, documentation-encouraged style that anchored a protected subtree with a trailing wildcard, e.g. "/admin/.*", will not match a request whose URL contains a line-terminator character after the protected prefix. If the servlet container passes through an encoded line terminator such as %0A or %0D (or a pathInfo/queryString value containing such a character) in the URL that this matcher sees, the intended security rule is not applied to that request while other parts of the framework may still route or serve it, i.e. a matcher-based authorization/security bypass. The root cause is the missing Pattern.DOTALL flag at compile time combined with full-string matches() semantics; the presence of Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE shows the author thought about flags but omitted DOTALL.

This is a candidate, not a confirmed vulnerability: whether it is exploitable depends on the deployed matcher patterns and on container-level URL handling, neither of which is visible in the read source.

title: SecureRandomFactoryBean weak/removeable entropy when a seed is configured
description: SecureRandomFactoryBean.getObject() creates a SecureRandom via SecureRandom.getInstance(algorithm). label: flash_high
title: DefaultRedirectResolver host matching accepts arbitrary subdomains (endsWith) and path prefixes
description:
DefaultRedirectResolver.redirectMatches compares the registered and requested hosts via hostMatches, which by default (matchSubdomains=true) returns requested.endsWith(registered) rather than an exact host equality. It also accepts the requested path when it merely startsWith the registered path (after StringUtils.cleanPath). ExactMatchRedirectResolver exists as a stricter alternative but DefaultRedirectResolver is the AuthorizationEndpoint default.

title: DefaultRedirectResolver trusts unregistered client-supplied redirect_uri (open redirect / code & token exposure)
description: DefaultRedirectResolver.resolveRedirect implements the redirect_uri authorization check. It throws a RedirectMismatchException only when the client has registered redirect URIs AND none of them match. If the client's registered redirect set is null or empty, the method simply returns the raw requestedRedirect supplied by the (unauthenticated) requester (line 79-81). It also, when registered URIs exist, returns the raw requested value whenever redirectMatches is true (obtainMatchingRedirect, line 155-156). This means for clients configured without a fixed redirect URI (or for which nothing is registered), an attacker controlling the authorize request can choose an arbitrary redirect target. The registered URI is the primary defense against authorization-code / access-token leakage and against open redirects, so trusting the attacker-supplied value is a security-relevant weakening. The default resolver is the one instantiated at AuthorizationEndpoint line 94, so this is the default behavior of the authorization server unless an administrator overrides it.

label: flash_max
title: DefaultRedirectResolver redirect matching uses host suffix, path prefix and ignores port
description: DefaultRedirectResolver.redirectMatches accepts a requested redirect if the protocol is equal, the host matches via hostMatches (which, with the default matchSubdomains=true, checks only requested.endsWith(registered)), and the cleaned requested path starts with the cleaned registered path. The Javadoc explicitly states 'the port is not matched'. Two consequences are security-relevant: (a) with matchSubdomains enabled, a registered host like 'example.com' also matches attacker-controlled hosts that merely end with that string (e.g. 'evilexample.com'), because endsWith is a raw suffix test rather than a label-aware comparison; (b) because the path check is a prefix test and the port/host are not strictly compared, redirect targets can resolve to an unintended origin/path. These looseness properties make the redirect target less tightly bound to the registered client, which matters for code/token delivery.

label: flash_max
title: SpelView evaluates resolved placeholder content as SpEL and the approval page does not HTML-escape scopes
description: SpelView.render builds the HTML view by taking the template and running it through a PropertyPlaceholderHelper whose PlaceholderResolver parses each ${...} placeholder as a SpEL expression and evaluates it against the model map (lines 51-57, 70-71). The resulting string is written directly to the response with contentType text/html and no output encoding (lines 72-73). WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint builds its template from model/request data without escaping: createScopes interpolates the raw scope name into the SCOPE HTML fragment via %scope% and %key% (lines 54-55, 71-72), and the model (including 'scopes') is populated from request-derived data (lines 21-26, 31-33). Separately, because placeholder values are evaluated as SpEL against a StandardEvaluationContext rooted at the model, any template value that is itself interpretable as a SpEL expression is evaluated; while the templates here are constants, this design makes the rendering sensitive to unescaped/untrusted model content.

label: flash_high
title: @Url parameter accepts an absolute URL, letting the caller override the configured base host
description: RequestFactory permits a method parameter annotated @Url without validating that the resolved URL stays within the Retrofit base URL. At request-build time, ParameterHandler.RelativeUrl writes the caller-supplied value into the URL builder (setRelativeUrl), and RequestBuilder later resolves it against the base URL via baseUrl.newBuilder(relativeUrl)/baseUrl.resolve(relativeUrl). Because OkHttp resolves an absolute URL argument against the base, a caller-controlled @Url value can redirect the request to an arbitrary host/scheme; the request destination is thus caller-influenced. The annotation parser accepts multiple types for @Url and performs no host allow-listing. This is a candidate for unintended destination override in applications that pass untrusted input into an @Url parameter, but it may equally be the documented, intended feature of @Url; whether it is a defect depends on application usage.

label: flash_max
title: Potential path traversal via @Path parameter substitution in RequestBuilder.addPathParam (no dot-segment canonicalization)
description: RequestBuilder.addPathParam builds the request relative URL by directly substituting the @Path value into the URL template: `relativeUrl = relativeUrl.replace("{" + name + "}", canonicalizeForPath(value, encoded));` (RequestBuilder.java:94). The only transformation applied to the value is character-level encoding in canonicalizeForPath (RequestBuilder.java:97-144), which percent-encodes control characters, characters in PATH_SEGMENT_ALWAYS_ENCODE_SET, and — only when alreadyEncoded is false — '/' and '%' (lines 101-103, 125-127). Dot characters ('.') are never in the encode set and are always passed through unchanged, and when alreadyEncoded is true (i.e. `@Path(..., encoded = true)`) slashes and percent signs are also passed through unchanged. Consequently a caller-supplied value such as ".." inserted into a template like "/api/{id}/data" yields "/api/../data", and with encoded=true a value containing "../" can introduce real path separators. title: Wildcard and regex type permissions translate patterns to regular expressions whose Unicode character classes are subtle, risking over-broad matching (configuration-correctness)

title: ZipUtil unpack callback builds target path from untrusted entry name without output-root containment check
description: Call chain: ZipUtil.unpack(File, File) at ZipUtil.java:938 -> unpack(File, File, NameMapper) at 994 -> iterate(zip, new Unpacker(...)) at 996. label: flash_max
title: ZIP extraction writes entry names without path containment (Zip Slip / path traversal)
description: The extraction callbacks build destination paths by concatenating the output directory with the raw archive entry name and then write/copy file content there, with no traversal check. In ZipUtil.Unpacker.process the name is produced by mapper.map(zipEntry.getName()) and used as `new File(outputDir, name)` (ZipUtil.java lines 1150-1163); directories are created via FileUtils.forceMkdir and files via FileUtils.copy(in, file). ZipUtil.BackslashUnpacker.process does the same for backslash-separated names, splitting the entry name into path segments and creating each segment directory before copying the final segment (lines 1208-1226). ZipUtil.Unwraper.process also uses `new File(outputDir, name)` (lines 1258-1270), and Zips.UnpackingCallback.process uses `new File(destination, entryName)` and writes via FileUtils.copy / transformIntoFile (Zips.java lines 675-700). No normalization or containment check exists: searches for `normalize` and `..` in main sources returned no matches, and the `getCanonicalPath` match is only in the unrelated FileUtilsV2_2 copy routine. Therefore an entry named e.g. `../../etc/cron.d/job` (or a name that resolves outside outputDir) causes the extracted file to be created outside the intended directory, potentially overwriting arbitrary writable files. Note java.util.zip.ZipEntry does not itself reject `..` path segments; the value originates from the archive. This is a candidate: the library is API-driven and no in-repo caller/endpoint proving remote reachability was located.

title: Extraction applies archive-supplied POSIX permissions to created files/directories
description: ZipEntryUtil.getZTFilePermissions reads the 'ASi Unix' extra field from each entry and returns a ZTFilePermissions object derived from the entry's mode bits (ZipEntryUtil.java lines 190-204 and 164-181, using AsiExtraField mode & 0777).
